look_here_first: FIRST photograph stem BASE: Engelmann’s sage has cauline (stem) leaves but no persistent basal-leaf set. Narrow linear leaf blades ~30–60 × 3–5 mm. THEN count flowers in axillary cymes (three per cyme) and examine the ten-ribbed 10–11 mm calyx with short awned tips. Tack-shaped subsessile glands require true macro; never pretend broad shot proves them.
project_tracker_diagnostic: Low dense perennial with only cauline narrow leaves, tack-shaped glandular hairs, repeated 3-flowered cymes, strongly 10-ridged awned calyces, and a pale strongly marked lower corolla lip.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays native list, Travis preserve records, UT Williamson County treatment, and Comal County herbarium material; no county presence inferred.

morphology_keys.habit: Perennial low dense clump with many stems.
morphology_keys.leaves: Only cauline narrow leaves; paired bases can form a short sheath across the node.
morphology_keys.inflorescence: 3-flowered cymes repeated at closely spaced nodes.
morphology_keys.calyx: Strongly 10-ridged with short awned lobe tips.
morphology_keys.floral_detail: Pale blue-violet corolla with a broad white/violet-marked lower lip.
morphology_keys.leaf_measurement: Cauline linear leaves typically ~30–60 mm long and 3–5 mm wide (UT Austin Williamson County morphology).
morphology_keys.calyx_measurement: Calyx ~10–11 mm long, 10-ridged with short ~0.5 mm awns and tack-shaped glands (microscope/strong macro needed).
morphology_keys.flower_group: Two opposite axillary cymes at each flowering node, typically 3 flowers per cyme.
morphology_keys.corolla: Blue-violet with conspicuous white/violet-marked lower lip; corolla approximately 18–22 mm (UT Austin); can overlap Texas sage.
morphology_keys.lookalike_first: Compare S. texana basal + stem leaf set and pitted (rather than tack-shaped) glands; both are low, blue-violet sages.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Texas sage has basal leaves and pitted/sunken glands. Azure sage is much taller and more open.

steps.question: Is there a real set of basal leaves?
steps.here: Engelmann: only cauline leaves; document the basal nodes, not just a cropped flowering shoot.
steps.confidence: high when a complete plant is visible

steps.question: Are blades narrow linear (~3–5 mm wide)?
steps.here: Engelmann: narrow linear cauline blades 30–60 × 3–5 mm. Some Texas sage leaves overlap; basal leaf shape is corroboration.

steps.question: Are there 3-flowered cymes in each opposite cluster?
steps.here: Engelmann: paired cymes, usually three florets each, along compact flowering axis. Need a good side-view with individual pedicels visible.

steps.question: Can you see 10 ribs and tiny awn points?
steps.here: Engelmann: calyx ~10–11 mm; 10 strong ribs and short ~0.5 mm awns. Texas sage calyx is also 10-ribbed and pointed; not decisive without glands.

steps.question: Are gland heads tack-shaped above the surface?
steps.here: Engelmann: raised tack-shaped subsessile glands; Texas sage: glands embedded in small pits. Requires verified original macro; none of these broad gallery photos resolve individual glands.

photo_diagnostic_lesson.memory_rule: Engelmann = stem leaves + groups of three + tack glands. Texas = basal leaves + pit glands.

mini_glossary.cyme: SIME — a little branching flower group
mini_glossary.verticil: VER-ti-sil — clustered blooms around a node, often made of two opposing cymes
mini_glossary.calyx: KAY-liks — the usually green outer cup surrounding the flower
mini_glossary.awn: AWN — a thin pointed extension at the end of a calyx tooth
mini_glossary.glandular_hair: A hair bearing a tiny sticky or aromatic gland at its tip.

diagnostic_photo_targets: Complete plant base with NO basal leaves (reproducible ID shot)
Three-flowered opposing axillary cymes, each pedicel visible
A leaf against mm ruler measuring 3–5 mm width
Calyx side/back with 10 ribs and short awns in good focus
Real micromacro of tack-shaped surface glands, with ruler and correctly located arrows
Matched S. texana pit-shaped leaf glands at SAME magnification
